title: A Good Strategy Is Always Evolving
author: Admired Leadership
summary: Opening with a Feynman-cited Buddhist proverb about the same key opening both heaven and hell, this article argues that a fixed strategy applied to a changing situation can produce wildly different outcomes because the obstacles a strategy must contend with are always evolving. It uses a cooking allegory — five chefs given the same recipe will produce five distinct meals — to illustrate that execution context matters as much as the plan itself. The piece criticizes leaders and organizations who set a strategy once and then simply watch it play out, arguing instead that the best leaders continuously tweak and adjust the strategy as conditions shift. It ends with a set of self-check questions meant to prompt leaders to assess whether their own strategy is genuinely dynamic or has quietly calcified.
points: A fixed strategy applied to changing conditions can produce very different outcomes over time.
Strategy is framed as the ongoing coordination of action against continuously emerging obstacles.
The five-chefs cooking allegory illustrates how context shapes outcomes as much as the plan itself.
Many leaders set a strategy once and then passively watch it play out rather than adjusting it.
The best leaders frequently tweak, adjust, and sometimes substantially revise their strategy as conditions change.
quotes: Every person “is given the key to the gates of heaven; the same key also opens the gates of hell.
In reality, strategy is the coordination of action against emerging obstacles.
Give five master chefs the same recipe and ingredients and they will produce five distinctive meals.
A strategy needs to evolve alongside the changing dynamics of the problem or opportunity.
The best leaders adjust, tweak, and alter the foundational strategy with great frequency.
There is no perfect strategy, nor a perfect leader who might perfect it.
